evidence.label: A counterexample to the Monge ansatz for the three-marginal Coulomb cost

headline: Proves that the best three-electron Coulomb arrangement need not follow fixed maps, even for a smooth density.
scope: Three-marginal optimal transport with Coulomb cost, where all three marginals equal one smooth density on ℝ³. Extensions cover inverse-power costs in every dimension d ≥ 2.
plain: Chemists study how electrons arrange themselves when their repulsion dominates. One model asks for the cheapest way to place three electrons, each spread by the same density, under Coulomb repulsion. A common guess says the best arrangement fixes the second and third electron once the first is placed. This paper builds a smooth density where no such fixed rule is optimal. Fixed rules can still get as close to the best cost as you like.
doesNot: This does not show that the guess fails for typical or physical densities from real atoms; it gives one constructed density. Lean covers only the three-dimensional Coulomb case.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles an open question about the co-motion ansatz in density functional theory, with a Lean statement of the three-dimensional Coulomb case.

explanation:
Start with three charged particles. The Coulomb cost of a triple is the sum of 1 over each pairwise distance. Put one particle at 0 and the others at e₁ and −e₁, one unit away on each side. The cost is 1 + 1 + 1/2 = 2.5. Now put them at 0, e₁ and e₂, two directions at right angles. The cost is 1 + 1 + 1/√2 ≈ 2.707. The first triple is cheaper. The triple 0, e₂, −e₂ costs 2.5 too.

Optimal transport here asks a question about a probability density, a rule for how mass spreads in space. Each of three electrons is spread by the same density. A plan is a joint rule for where all three sit at once. We want the plan with the least average cost. A Monge plan is a special plan: the first electron's position fixes the other two through maps. The guess that the best plan is a Monge plan is the Monge, or co-motion, ansatz. It comes from the strong-interaction limit of density functional theory, a method for computing electron behaviour[4].

For two electrons, Cotar, Friesecke and Klüppelberg proved an optimal map always exists[6]. Colombo and Di Marino showed that maps get as close to the best cost as you like[5]. Friesecke still listed the three-electron question as open in January 2026[7].

The paper claims a smooth density where no pair of maps reaches the minimum[1]. The density has five small blobs: one near 0 and one near each of ±e₁ and ±e₂. The triples (0, e_k, −e_k) have the same cost and the same pull at the centre[9]. So every best plan uses two families of triples, one along e₁ and one along e₂. The centre blob holds mass 1/3 and each outer blob holds 1/6. Suppose a map picks the e₁ family on a set S of the centre. It sends mass ν(S)/3 into a region holding only ν(S)/6[10]. That breaks the rule that each electron has the same density. So a best plan must split each point between the families, and no fixed map can. The idea adapts a splitting trick of Gerolin, Kausamo and Rajala[8].

Even so, the best cost over maps equals the true minimum; it is just never reached[2]. The paper extends this to inverse-power costs in every dimension at least 2[3].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the three-dimensional Coulomb result. So the paper proves it, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. The other powers and dimensions are not in the Lean scope. No specialist review of the paper is published.
hypeCheck: A solid counterexample with a Lean statement of the Coulomb case in three dimensions. It uses one constructed density, so it says nothing about typical physical densities. No specialist review is published.
